title: Alibaba unveils Qwen3.8-Max, a 2.4-trillion-parameter open-weight MoE model
subtitle: The first Max-class Qwen to be open-sourced activates 95 billion parameters per token, ships text-image-video input, and lands the API today with weights promised on Hugging Face next week.
author: AESOP AI Engine
body: Alibaba's Qwen team announced Qwen3.8-Max on August 3, a mixture-of-experts model with 2.4 trillion total parameters and roughly 95 billion activated per token. The model accepts text, images, and video, handles a one-million-token context window, and is aimed at autonomous coding and long-horizon agent tasks. It is available today through Alibaba Cloud's DashScope API, and the company said it will publish the full weights on Hugging Face and ModelScope the following week. Qwen3.8-Max returns fluent multimodal output — text answers grounded in the visual and video inputs — and Alibaba pitched it as directly competitive with the top OpenAI, Anthropic, and Google models on coding and reasoning benchmarks.

The news matters because this is the first Max-class Qwen model to ship as open weights. Alibaba kept its top-tier releases proprietary through most of 2026, and this release is a public reversal of that stance. It also comes two weeks after Moonshot released Kimi K3 at 2.8 trillion parameters — meaning China now has two openly downloadable models above the two-trillion threshold, both routed sparsely so they can actually be served on hardware people own. Alibaba said daily developer traffic on Qwen APIs has grown sharply since the Kimi K3 announcement, and pricing pressure inside China's model market appears to be pulling flagship weights into the open.

The broader context is a two-track frontier. US labs — OpenAI, Anthropic, Google — are keeping their strongest models behind APIs and pursuing a services and infrastructure business model. Chinese labs — Alibaba, Moonshot, DeepSeek, Meituan, Zhipu — are converging on a strategy of open-weight releases at the top end plus paid inference for the customers who don't want to run the model themselves. Enterprises hedging against a single-vendor lock-in now have a much stronger open-weight option than they did six months ago, and every regulator working on export controls or model registration has a harder problem than the one they scoped in 2025.

For learners: parameter counts are a headline, not the metric that matters. A 2.4-trillion MoE that fires only 95 billion parameters per token is not the same computational object as a dense 2.4-trillion model — sparse routing keeps inference cost tractable, which is exactly why releasing weights at this size is now possible. When you compare model announcements, look for three numbers together: total parameters, active parameters per token, and context window. Those three, plus the license, tell you whether a model is a research artifact or something you could actually deploy.
